Notebook.Title: OOM Killer: Memory, GC, and the Process Model

Section.Title: Welcome
Section.Paragraph: This is a live notebook, not a slideshow. Every CodeCell below is compiled and run by an actual Roslyn compiler at the moment you press Run — the same compiler that builds this project, running Sia's own [Sia] source generators against whatever you type. Change a number, add a Console.WriteLine, break something on purpose: it recompiles and reruns, nothing here is precomputed.

Every cell below declares the same Scope="oom-killer", which is what makes them share one program: pressing Run on any cell compiles and executes every cell in that scope up to and including it as a single unit. The first cell creates world once — every later cell in the scope reuses that same instance, and any class, struct, or system a cell declares is directly visible, unqualified, to every cell after it. (A cell with no Scope attribute at all is the opposite: its own fully independent program, sharing nothing with anything else — that's a per-notebook authoring choice, not a rule.)

One consequence of sharing a scope: Run always recompiles and replays that scope's cells from the top, since there is no way to keep a compiled program's execution paused between separate button clicks. Running a later cell re-shows fresh output for everything before it too. Compile checks a cell (and everything before it, in its scope) for errors without running anything; Stop is best-effort — it asks a runaway cell to give up at its next opportunity, but nothing in .NET can safely force a stuck loop to stop, so a pathological while(true){} may keep spinning in the background even after the UI moves on.

Section.Title: Scene 1: The Memory Leak
Section.Paragraph: Every process in this simulation carries a Memory component tracking used space against a limit. A [Sia]-annotated field like [Sia] int Used gets a generated Memory.View wrapper with a property setter — that is what lets other code write view.Used += 5 instead of manually re-inserting the whole struct.

List.Item: Memory.LeakRate — bytes leaked into Used per tick.
Memory.GcRate — bytes a garbage collector reclaims per tick.
When Used reaches Limit, an OOM-killer system steps in and destroys the entity — there is no negotiation.

Section.Paragraph: Try it: raise LeakRate above GcRate and the process dies faster; raise GcRate high enough and it survives indefinitely.

Section.Title: Scene 2: Scheduling Onto a Contended Core
Section.Paragraph: [Sia] properties do more than wrap a setter: assigning through the generated view raises a matching event — setting CoreAffinity.View.Core raises a CoreAffinity.SetCore event a system can subscribe to with EventUnion.Of<CoreAffinity.SetCore>(). Systems only run when something they actually care about changed.

Section.Title: Scene 3: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL
Section.Paragraph: Events can be cancelled. SignalTermSystem listens for a Term event but is filtered by EventUnion.Of<HOEvents.Cancel<Term>>() — if a cancel for that same event was also sent, the system is skipped entirely for that tick. That models the difference between SIGTERM (a process can trap and ignore it) and SIGKILL (a direct entity.Destroy(), which nothing can intercept).

Section.Title: Scene 4: Two Daemons Fight Over a Lock File
Section.Paragraph: Not every interaction needs a system — this cell computes damage directly, outside of any SystemBase, just to show that [Sia] views are ordinary structs you can use anywhere, not only from inside a query loop.

From here: try adding a third combatant, or give one of them a GcRate-style regeneration system from Scene 1. Nothing you change in this notebook can affect the rest of the Sia.NET codebase — you are only ever compiling a disposable, in-memory program.
